extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for applying pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102 novelty standards (anticipation, public use, on-sale, publications) including tests for range disclosures, public accessibility, derivation, and the 1-year grace period.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient specificity for range anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: When a prior-art reference discloses a range that touches or overlaps the claimed range, anticipation requires that the reference disclose the claimed subject matter with 'sufficient specificity' to constitute anticipation under the statute; this is a case-by-case determination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether the reference teaches the narrow claimed range with sufficient specificity (e.g., lack of evidence of criticality across the range supports anticipation — ClearValue) or whether the claimed range is shown to be critical and the reference's broader range does not clearly disclose the species (Atofina). If insufficient specificity exists, the reference might not anticipate but could be relevant to obviousness. If unclear, a combined 35 U.S.C. 102/103 rejection is permitted and the examiner must provide reasons for anticipation and a reasoned statement regarding obviousness. See MPEP § 2144.05 for obviousness of ranges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-overlapping close ranges do not anticipate
rubrics_metrics.description: A prior-art value or range that is very close to but does not touch or overlap the claimed range does not anticipate the claimed range under § 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires exact disclosure of what is claimed; differences between the reference and claim require evaluation under § 103. Example: Titanium Metals — a data point close but not equal to claimed composition did not anticipate though it was relevant to obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Secondary considerations irrelevant to § 102
rubrics_metrics.description: Evidence of secondary considerations (e.g., unexpected results, commercial success) is irrelevant to 35 U.S.C. 102 rejections and cannot overcome a rejection based solely on anticipation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secondary considerations may be relevant to nonobviousness under § 103, but they do not negate a novelty-based (§ 102) rejection. See In re Wiggins.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonanalogous art or teaching away not relevant to anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Arguments that a reference is nonanalogous art, teaches away, or addresses a different problem are not germane to a § 102 anticipation analysis; a reference may anticipate even if it disparages or teaches away from the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation focuses on whether the reference explicitly or inherently discloses every claim limitation. Teaching away or different field/context does not prevent anticipation (see Twin Disc, Celeritas, Atlas Powder, Upsher-Smith).

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA § 102(a) statutory elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. 102(a), an invention is unpatentable if it was known or used by others in this country, or patented or described in a printed publication in this or a foreign country, before the invention by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply definitions and subtests for each statutory phrase ('known or used', 'in this country', 'by others', 'patented or described in a printed publication') as discussed in MPEP § 2132 et seq.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'Known or used' means publicly known or used
rubrics_metrics.description: The statutory phrase 'known or used by others' means knowledge or use that is accessible to the public (i.e., not deliberately kept secret).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess public accessibility; see MPEP § 2128 for case law on what constitutes a 'printed publication' and public accessibility (Carella, W.L. Gore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Sale of product made by secret process
rubrics_metrics.description: Another’s sale of a product produced by a secret process can be a § 102(a) public use only if the process can be determined by examining the product.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If inspection of the sold product would not reveal the process, secret use coupled with sale does not create a public-use bar for the process claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: 'In this country' means within the United States
rubrics_metrics.description: For pre-AIA § 102(a) rejections, the knowledge or use relied upon must be in the United States.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Foreign knowledge or use, even if widespread abroad, cannot be the basis for a pre-AIA § 102(a) rejection (see In re Ekenstam). Changes to other statutes do not alter this meaning for pre-AIA § 102(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 'By others' means any different inventive entity
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'others' refers to any author(s) or inventor(s) different from the inventive entity — differing by even one person suffices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applies to publications, public knowledge/use; supports availability of the one-year grace period under § 102(b) if authorship differs (In re Katz).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prima facie case from publications 'by others'
rubrics_metrics.description: A prima facie case under pre-AIA § 102(a) is established if a printed publication by others describes the invention (or obvious variant) within one year of the filing date.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the reference is a U.S. patent or certain international publications within the year, make appropriate § 102(e) rejections; see MPEP § 2136 for § 102(e) case law and MPEP § 2128 for printed publication analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rebuttal by showing derivation from inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Applicant can rebut a prima facie § 102(a) case by showing the reference’s disclosure was derived from the inventor or at least one joint inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use disclaiming affidavits or specific inventor declarations to show the publication described the inventor’s own work (In re Katz, Ex parte Hirschler). If co-authors refuse to disclaim inventorship or provide contrary evidence, the rebuttal may fail (Ex parte Kroger). Adding coauthors as inventors is another possibility if statutory requirements are met.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 1.131 affidavits to antedate references
rubrics_metrics.description: When a reference is not a statutory bar under §§ 102(b)-(d), an applicant may overcome a § 102(a) rejection by submitting an affidavit under 37 C.F.R. § 1.131 to antedate the reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions and required evidence for Rule 131 affidavits are governed by case law (In re Foster, In re Facius) and MPEP § 715; alternative is a § 1.132 affidavit to show derivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-AIA § 102(b) one-year grace period rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Under pre-AIA § 102(b), an invention is barred if patented, described in a printed publication, in public use, or on sale more than one year prior to the U.S. application date; the one-year grace period is extended to the next working day if it would otherwise end on a holiday or weekend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The time bar is measured from the U.S. filing date. Continuation-in-part filings get the child filing date for claims not supported by the parent. See In re Katz, Paperless Accounting v. BART, and MPEP § 706.02 for effective filing date issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant's own pre-grace disclosures can be prior art under § 102(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s disclosure that became publicly available more than one year before the filing date is prior art under § 102(b) even if authored by the applicant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once disclosed beyond the grace period, the inventor has dedicated the idea to the public and cannot obtain a patent (De Graffenried, Bonito Boats).

rubrics_metrics.name: § 102(b) creates a statutory bar not overcome by affidavits
rubrics_metrics.description: A § 102(b) rejection (outside the one-year grace period) cannot be overcome by Rule 131 affidavits, foreign priority dates, or evidence that the applicant invented the subject matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Outside the grace period, the statutory bar is absolute (In re Foster).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and on-sale are distinct statutory bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Pre-AIA § 102(b) contains several distinct bars (publication, public use, on-sale); public use and on-sale may overlap but each can apply independently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether activity constitutes a public use, an on-sale bar, or both. Noncommercial/public-use distinctions and experimental-use considerations affect outcomes; see MPEP § 2133.03 subsections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy considerations underlying public-use/on-sale bars
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies: (A) promote prompt, widespread disclosure via patents; (B) prevent commercial exploitation beyond the statutory period; (C) discourage removal of inventions from the public domain that the public believes are freely available.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These policies inform analysis of public use and on-sale bar questions (RCA Corp. v. Data Gen., Manville Sales Corp.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Test for public use (accessibility/commercial exploitation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The public-use prong arises where the invention was accessible to the public or commercially exploited before the critical date; the test considers evidence relevant to experimentation, nature of activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, and commercial exploitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the Pfaff two-part test components separately (public use and ready-for-patenting). Commercial exploitation strongly indicates public use but requires context (Invitrogen). Even a single well-defined public use can bar patenting (Egbert).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public knowledge is not automatically public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Mere public knowledge of an invention does not automatically constitute a § 102(b) public use; § 102(b) bars public use or sale, not mere knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public knowledge might support a § 102(a) rejection but not necessarily a § 102(b) bar (TP Labs.). Evaluate facts against statutory elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Commercial vs. noncommercial use and secrecy
rubrics_metrics.description: Secret or confidential use alone does not necessarily avoid a public-use bar if the inventor commercially exploits the invention; noncommercial and commercial contexts may be treated differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether the use was for commercial exploitation or internal development; secret internal use without sales may not create a public-use bar (Invitrogen), but commercial exploitation coupled with secrecy can. See distinctions in MPEP § 2133.03(c) and (e).

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-secret use is not ipso facto public use
rubrics_metrics.description: Non-secret (not hidden) use does not automatically equal public use; courts examine totality of circumstances including control, access, and confidentiality obligations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider whether inventor retained control, restricted access, or imposed confidentiality; absence or presence of confidentiality agreements is one factor but not determinative (TP Labs., Bernhardt, Moleculon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Display or use in public view (even if hidden in larger article)
rubrics_metrics.description: If an inventor puts a machine or article embodying the invention in public view or sells it in a way accessible to the public, that can constitute public use even if the claimed inventive features are hidden within a larger machine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public accessibility of the larger article suffices; observers need not understand inner workings to trigger public use (In re Blaisdell, Ex parte Kuklo, Hall v. MacNeale).

rubrics_metrics.name: Private personal use is not public use
rubrics_metrics.description: An inventor's private use limited to locations with reasonable expectation of privacy and for personal enjoyment is not a public use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate evidence of control and privacy (Moleculon Research). Private demonstrations to close friends in a private setting typically do not create a public-use bar.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor allowing another to use without restriction equals public use
rubrics_metrics.description: An invention is in public use if the inventor permits another to use it without limitation, restriction, or obligation of secrecy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even absent a formal confidentiality agreement, lack of restrictions or obligations indicates public use (In re Smith, Ex parte C). Contracts and the nature of the relationship are relevant.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use by independent third parties that informs the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsecret use by an independent third party can be a public use if it sufficiently informs the public of the invention, or if a competitor could reasonably ascertain the invention (including when details can be ascertained by inspecting products made by the process).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the third-party use disclosed enough detail to inform competitors or the public; secret third-party use can still be public if details are ascertainable by inspection or analysis of products (Bird Provision, cases cited).
